text: Chapter 6's config-driven script already separated settings from code. Secrets need that same treatment, but more carefully — a leaked password or API key isn't just an inconvenience, it's a real security incident.

This is the pattern to never write: a connection string with the actual production password typed right into the script. If that file ever gets committed to a shared repo, backed up somewhere, or just read by someone over your shoulder, the production password is exposed, full stop.

os dot environ reads a value the operating system is holding in memory for the running process — it's never written anywhere in the script itself. And using square-bracket access instead of dot-get means a missing variable raises a clear KeyError immediately, rather than silently proceeding with no password at all.

For local development, python-dotenv lets you keep secrets in a .env file — which absolutely gets added to .gitignore — and load_dotenv reads that file straight into os.environ. The payoff is that the rest of your code never changes: it reads from os.environ the same way whether the value came from your laptop's .env file or from production's real environment.

Not every setting deserves the same treatment. A missing database password should raise a RuntimeError and stop the script cold — that's Lesson 41's fail-loud principle, applied to configuration. But a missing retry limit can reasonably fall back to a sensible default with os.environ.get, instead of crashing over something that minor.

That wraps up Chapter 7 — logging, testing, error handling, scheduling, and now secrets, the full toolkit for running a pipeline unattended and trusting it. Chapter 8 shifts gears entirely: you'll meet PySpark and SparkSession, and start scaling pipelines beyond what a single machine can handle.
